name: Adam Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that doesn't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a stockman, well, a trainee stockman, at Ferris Farms. It's around eight hundred pigs from weaners to finishers, plus maize and wheat that mostly goes back into feed. The feeding is already automatic, so my day is walking the sheds, checking water lines, spotting sick pigs, washing pens, and fighting the feed computer when it sulks. Before this I spent eleven years in a parcel warehouse until the sorting robots came in, so I've been on the wrong end of automation once already.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up on a pig farm from a warehouse?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A mate of mine, Dariusz, worked here and said they needed someone who wasn't scared of the computer. I'm slow with the actual pigs still, my boss Linda says I look at a pig like it's a spreadsheet. But I use AI every day, I photograph a pig with a cough and ask it what it might be before I bother the vet. Pay's low, Nadia works part-time at the pharmacy, we've got Leo and Eva, and our savings would last about three weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, honestly. I'd post something like, the tools are useful, they just weren't magic, and the jobs problem is still a pay problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine. I'd keep using AI the way I do, it saves me twenty minutes a day on paperwork and helps me learn the pigs faster. The machine I'm actually scared of is the one that already took my warehouse job, and that one's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Ferris and keep pushing Linda to let me run the feed data properly. I'd look at doing the pig health certificate at the college online this winter. Maybe pick up a bit of extra money setting up farm software for neighbours, I've done it once for a beef farmer down the lane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, because I like new things, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the jobs problem is still a pay problem. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mean pig work is hard, early and pays badly, and that's not because of computers. It's because the processors and supermarkets hold all the cards. I'm in the union, I'd like to see sector-wide pay rates for farm work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much did the beef farmer pay you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two hundred and a leg of lamb, oddly, given he's beef. It took me a Saturday. If I could do one a month, that's a car repair or school shoes covered.

S0.say: He'd say he's a bit disappointed: the tools are useful but not magic. He'd frame the jobs problem as a pay problem rooted in processors and supermarkets.
S0.think: Privately he's fine, since AI saves him paperwork time and helps him learn. The automation that really scares him is the kind that already took his warehouse job.
S0.do: Keeps working at the pig unit and pushes his boss to let him run the feed data. Studies for a pig health certificate online this winter and does occasional paid farm-software setups for neighbours.
S0.feel: Calm, a little flat because he enjoys new things.
S0.quote: The machine I'm actually scared of is the one that already took my warehouse job, and that one's real.
S0.fieldNote: He separates useful AI tools from physical automation, which he has felt directly. His progressive views show up as a call for sector-wide farm pay. Already finding small side income from his tech comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the chance for farm workers to get trained up and paid more, if the government funds it. I'd be the one at work saying, don't fear it, learn it, but also don't let the owner keep all the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it could be good for me. Ferris will automate more, washing robots, camera monitoring for sick pigs, and somebody has to make all that work together. I'm the only one there under fifty who isn't scared of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Linda straight away I want to be the person who runs the new systems, and I'd ask for a pay rise to go with it. I'd finish the pig health certificate and look at a short course on farm robotics. I'd keep doing software setups on Saturdays, maybe two a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly, with a bit of guilt about Dariusz, who hates computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the guilt.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dariusz got me this job. He's brilliant with pigs, he can tell a pig's off from the way it stands, and he can't stand screens. If the farm needs one less person and one more screen-person, I know which of us stays, and he's my friend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd teach him, if he'd let me, half an hour at lunch. And I'd argue for the farm to keep him on as the pig expert, because the cameras will miss things. Whether Linda listens depends on the price of pork.

S1.say: He'd say this is the chance for farm workers to be trained and paid more, if the government funds it. At work he'd urge people to learn the tools but not let owners keep all the savings.
S1.think: Privately he thinks steady change could be good for him, as the one younger worker at the unit comfortable with technology. He expects to become the person who makes new systems work.
S1.do: Asks his boss right away to make him responsible for new systems, with a pay rise. Finishes the pig health certificate, takes a short farm robotics course and does about two software setups a month on Saturdays.
S1.feel: Excited, with guilt about a friend who hates computers.
S1.quote: If the farm needs one less person and one more screen-person, I know which of us stays, and he's my friend.
S1.fieldNote: His adaptability turns steady disruption into an opportunity, despite thin savings. The emotional weight sits with his colleague, not himself. He wants to protect the friend's role as the animal expert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a basic income and public ownership of the big systems, because otherwise a handful of companies own everything. I'd post that every day and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's bad for me. My whole plan was to be the robot guy, and if the robots can run themselves in two years there's no robot guy. Three weeks of savings and a mortgage, that's a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI to go through every bill and benefit we could claim, that week. I'd try to squeeze every bit of cash out of the next year, extra shifts, setups, selling the second car. And I'd join whatever campaign was pushing for an income, I'd be organising it in the village if nobody else was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the warehouse again, but with no next door to walk through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having two years change things compared with the steady picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady change rewards people like me, because I learn fast. Two years doesn't reward anybody except whoever owns the machines. Being quick doesn't help when the whole race is over before lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leo and Eva?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leo's eleven, he'd already know from his phone. I'd tell him we'll be all right because we'll stick together and fight for a fair deal. Eva's seven, she'd just want to know if she can still visit the piglets.

S2.say: He'd call for a basic income and public ownership of the big AI systems, so a few companies don't own everything. He'd post this daily.
S2.think: Privately he sees two-year AGI as bad for him, because his plan to become the robot specialist disappears. With three weeks of savings and a mortgage, he faces a cliff.
S2.do: Uses AI that week to check every bill and benefit the family could claim. Works extra shifts and setups, sells the second car, and organises a local campaign for an income guarantee.
S2.feel: Like losing the warehouse job again, with no next door to walk through.
S2.quote: Being quick doesn't help when the whole race is over before lunch.
S2.fieldNote: Speed cancels out his main strength. He notices that rapid change rewards only owners, not fast learners. His response is energetic and collective rather than despairing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to build the safety net and we'd better start now. I'd be pushing the union to get farm workers a seat in whatever talks happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is long enough for my plan to work for a while and short enough that it ends. I'd probably have three good years running Ferris's systems, then who knows. That's not nothing, it pays down debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go hard at the robotics course in year one and get Linda to put me in charge of the first machines. I'd put every bit of extra pay into the mortgage and the car loan, aiming to be out of the car loan by year two. I'd keep a list, honestly, of other things I could do when it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but sharp. Like a deadline at work, you get focused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's on that list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anything where people want a person. Training other farmers on the systems, maybe, for a while. Nadia's at the pharmacy and keeps saying people still want to talk to someone about their pills. I'd write the list with the AI, which is a bit funny when you think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years against two. What's the real difference for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five, I get paid for being early before it all lands, and I can clear some debt. With two I never get paid for it at all. Three years of decent wages is the difference between losing the house and not.

S3.say: He'd say five years is the time to build the safety net and start now. He'd push the union for a seat for farm workers in any talks.
S3.think: Privately he sees five years as enough for his plan to pay off for about three years before it ends. Those years would let him pay down debt.
S3.do: Takes the robotics course hard in year one and gets put in charge of the first machines. Puts every extra bit of pay into the mortgage and car loan, aiming to clear the car loan by year two, and keeps a list of fallback work.
S3.feel: Anxious but sharp and focused, like facing a deadline.
S3.quote: I'd write the list with the AI, which is a bit funny when you think about it.
S3.fieldNote: He values the middle timeline in plain money terms: three years of better pay could save the house. He is honest that his advantage is temporary. Using AI to plan life after AI amuses him rather than troubling him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift, and we'd be fools not to use it for a fair transition. Farm towns need their own plan, not just whatever the cities get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is the one where I come out ahead for a while. I'd be fifty-three at the end, mortgage much smaller, kids nearly grown. Even if the work dries up after that, we'd be standing on firmer ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build up the side business into something real, setting up and fixing systems for farms in the valley, maybe with Dariusz as the animal side. I'd do the courses one by one, and save properly for the first time in my life. I'd keep pushing for an income guarantee long before it's needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful, with a small knot of worry about what comes after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A business with thin savings is a risk. Would you really do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small, yes. Not a van and a logo, just evenings and Saturdays until it pays more than the farm. I've got nothing to lose that I'd not lose anyway in this picture, and I'd be good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What comes after, in that knot of worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After the decade, the systems fix themselves, and then what am I for? I'd like to think I'll be teaching my grandkids to hold a piglet, not explaining why nobody needs me.

S4.say: He'd call a decade a gift that must be used for a fair transition. Farm towns need their own plan rather than whatever cities get.
S4.think: Privately he expects to come out ahead for a while with ten years, ending at fifty-three with a smaller mortgage and grown children. Even if work dries up later, his family would be on firmer ground.
S4.do: Grows his side business setting up and fixing farm systems in the valley, possibly with his friend on the animal side. Takes courses one at a time, saves properly for the first time, and campaigns early for an income guarantee.
S4.feel: Mostly hopeful, with a small knot of worry about what he is for afterwards.
S4.quote: I'd like to think I'll be teaching my grandkids to hold a piglet, not explaining why nobody needs me.
S4.fieldNote: The decade lets his adaptability pay off, though he knows the end point still removes his role. He frames the business small and low-risk because of thin savings. His lingering worry is about purpose, not just money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because being quick is all I've got, and it wouldn't matter. What would help is an income floor that's there before the jobs go, not after. And public say in who owns these systems.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what they lost last time. I lost a warehouse job and nobody asked me anything, they just gave me a leaflet. I'm the guy who loves the tech and I'm still saying: put the safety net up before you knock the ladder away.

headlineQuote: I'm the guy who loves the tech and I'm still saying: put the safety net up before you knock the ladder away.
portrait: Adam Moreau is a 43-year-old trainee stockman at an 800-pig unit who came to farming after warehouse robots took his job of eleven years. He uses AI every day, lives with his partner Nadia, a part-time pharmacy worker, and two children, with about three weeks of savings. Progressive and pro-union, he sees steady change as his chance to become the farm's systems person, but two-year AGI wipes out that advantage and alarms him. With five or ten years, his plan is to earn well while it lasts, clear debt and build a small setup business. He wants a safety net before jobs disappear.
biggestWorry: AGI within two years, because his only advantage is learning fast and that would count for nothing.
whatWouldHelp: An income floor put in place before jobs go, and public say over who owns the AI systems.
